country.comment: Conducted in Mandala, an urban slum in M-East Ward, Mumbai, Maharashtra, India.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title & Abstract; PDF p. 5, Section II.a; PDF p. 19, Section V

effect_estimate.comment: All regression models adjusted for household size, monthly income per capita, and religion; religion and income were not statistically significantly associated with water quantity after adjusting for legal status.
effect_estimate.value: In multivariate linear regression (N = 593 households), non-notified households used 37.3% fewer litres per capita per day (LPCD) of water than notified households (95% CI: -46.4%, -26.5%; p < 0.001; unadjusted difference: -38.2%, p < 0.001), corresponding to median consumption of 17.7 LPCD (IQR: 10.7-34.1) in non-notified vs. 31.4 LPCD (IQR: 17.6-51.7) in notified households (p < 0.0001). In multivariate logistic regression, non-notified households had 3.4 higher adjusted odds of consuming <=20 LPCD than notified households. Non-notified households were also significantly less likely to have an in-home water tap (2.6% vs. 9.9%; primary mode p < 0.001), paid higher median water costs (407 vs. 219 INR/1,000 litres; p < 0.001) and median share of monthly income on water (11% [IQR: 6-20] vs. 9% [IQR: 5-17]; p = 0.01), obtained water less frequently (<3 times/week: 49.0% vs. 26.5%; p < 0.001), differed in sanitation method (open defecation 4.5% vs. 2.1%; pay community toilet 82.9% vs. 91.9%; p = 0.005), and missed or were late to work more often due to water collection (30.3% vs. 22.6%; p = 0.03). In GSEM path analysis, infrastructure mode, accessibility, reliability, and cost mediated 38.7% of the association between non-notified status and water quantity (remaining direct difference: -23.4%).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 10, Table 1; PDF p. 11, Section III.a & Figure 2; PDF pp. 12-16, Sections III.b-III.c, Table 2, Table 3 & Figure 3

mechanism_certainty.comment: Analytical cross-sectional design (ceiling of 2). Assigned 1 because the primary empirical study documents strong statistical and GIS spatial associations (and an exploratory statistical mediation pathway) between neighbourhood notification classification and water infrastructure/access/quantity/cost/reliability, while the administrative operationalization of legal exclusion (pre-2000 proof-of-residence documentation rules, group tap applications, and municipal discretion) is contextualized from statutory/secondary sources rather than directly observed at the administrative decision level.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 4-5, Section I.c; PDF pp. 8-9, Section II.d; PDF pp. 11-16, Section III, Tables 2-3 & Figures 2-3; PDF p. 18, Section IV

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines legal slum recognition ('notification') under the Maharashtra Slum Areas Act of 1971 requiring pre-2000 residence proof documentation (e.g., voter ID) and location on state/city rather than central government or private land, neighbourhood-level exclusion from municipal piped service infrastructure, group community-tap application requirements, informal payments and long/unsuccessful application delays, municipal officials' discretion in treating neighbourhoods as non-notified and approving applications, and Bombay High Court public interest litigation (Pani Haq Samiti).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, ENFORCEMENT, tenure, documentation, property, service_area, procedural_steps, fees, delay, discretion, judicial_review
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 4-5, Section I.c; PDF p. 11, Figure 2; PDF p. 17, Section IV

outcome_flags.comment: Measures in-home and shared municipal community tap connections, GIS coverage within a 10m tap radius, primary/secondary modes of water access and collection time/crowding, sanitation method (Table 1), frequency of obtaining water per week (reliability) and tap flow functionality/intermittency (continuity), water consumption in LPCD and days of insufficient water (quantity), and water price per 1,000L plus share of monthly household income spent on water (affordability). Microbiological water quality was explicitly not measured (PDF p. 18).
outcome_flags.value: formal_connection, water_access, sanitation_access, service_coverage, service_reliability, service_quantity, affordability, service_continuity

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Primary quantitative analytical cross-sectional household survey comparing notified and non-notified slum neighbourhoods using multivariable linear/logistic regression and path analysis without a quasi-experimental intervention comparator (data were collected prior to implementation of the Bombay High Court order; authors explicitly note cross-sectional design on PDF p. 18).

risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF p. 5, Section I.c; PDF pp. 7-9, Sections II.c-II.d; PDF p. 18, Section IV

sample_size.comment: 600 households were randomly selected from a census of 2,203 enumerated households across Matangrushi Nagar (1,285 households) and Indira Nagar (918 households); 7 were excluded for missing key water variables, yielding N = 593 analysed households (283 notified, 310 non-notified; child school-absence subsample N = 376 households with children). Public community water taps across both neighbourhoods were also GIS-mapped.
sample_size.value: 593 households analysed across 2 neighbourhoods (283 households in notified Matangrushi Nagar and 310 households in non-notified Indira Nagar; 600 households initially surveyed, 7 excluded for missing data)
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 5, Section II.a; PDF pp. 7-8, Sections II.c-II.d; PDF pp. 9-10, Section III.a & Table 1; PDF p. 14, Table 2

study_design.comment: Data were collected March-May 2016 using random sampling from a complete neighbourhood household enumeration, two-week container enumeration for water consumption, GIS mapping of community water taps, and multivariable regression and GSEM mediation analysis.
study_design.value: Cross-sectional representative household survey and GIS infrastructure mapping with bivariate tests, multivariate linear and logistic regression, and GSEM path analysis
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 2, Section I.a; PDF pp. 7-9, Sections II.c-II.d; PDF p. 18, Section IV
